•	Court Martial Appeals: Authority to quash, confirm, or modify sentences, and order retrials.
5.	Procedure & Exclusions
•	Precedent Requirement: Exhaustion of internal remedies before appeal.
•	Procedure: Detailed rules for hearings, evidence, and decision-making.
•	Jurisdiction Exclusion: Civil courts (except the Supreme Court) are barred.
•	Good Faith Protection: For actions taken under the Act.

Summary of the General Clauses Act, 1897

Key Features
•	Definitions: Explains terms such as "Central Government," "State Government," "person," "immovable property," "movable property," "document," "month," and others.
•	Computation of Time: Sets rules for calculating time periods prescribed under laws.
•	Powers and Appointments: States that the power to appoint a person generally includes the power to suspend or dismiss that person, unless a law provides otherwise.
•	Power to Issue Orders: A power to issue notifications, rules, or orders generally includes the power to amend, vary, or rescind them.
•	Repeal and Re-enactment: Provides rules on what happens when a law is repealed or replaced, including protection of rights, liabilities, penalties, and legal proceedings that arose under the repealed law unless the new law indicates otherwise.
•	Gender and Number: Unless the context requires otherwise:
•	Words in the masculine gender include females.
•	Words in the singular include the plural, and vice versa.
•	Meaning of "Person": Includes individuals, companies, associations, and bodies of individuals.
•	Official Powers: Clarifies how powers conferred on public authorities should be exercised.

dc.identifier.next_section.value: 106.Legacy does not lapse if one of two joint legatees die before testator.

dc.identifier.section_page_note.value:
(1) If the legatee does not survive the testator, the legacy cannot take effect, but shall lapse and form part of the residue of the testator's property, unless it appears by the Will that the testator intended that it should go to some other person.
(2) In order to entitle the representatives of the legatee to receive the legacy, it must be proved that he survived the testator.
Illustrations
(i) The testator bequeaths to B "500 rupees which B owes me". B dies before the testator; the legacy lapses.
(ii) A bequest is made to A and his children. A dies before the testator, or happens to be dead when the will is made. The legacy to A and his children lapses.
(iii) A legacy is given to A, and, in case of his dying before the testator, to B. A dies before the testator. The legacy goes to B.
(iv) A sum of money is bequeathed to A for life, and after his death to B. A dies in the lifetime of the testator; B survives the testator. The bequest to B takes effect.
(v) A sum of money is bequeathed to A on his completing his eighteenth year, and in case he should die before he completes his eighteenth year, to B. A completes his eighteenth year, and dies in the lifetime of the testator. The legacy to A lapses, and the bequest to ii does not take effect.
(vi) The testator and the legatee perished in the same ship-wreck. There is no evidence to show which died first. The legacy lapses.
